1.1.
Let's study the effect of quantum defect more carefully, and connect it with practical limitations related to power scaling of high-power lasers. We consider a few very common laser gain media: titanium-doped sapphire (Ti:Sapph), neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG), ytterbium-doped YAG (Yb:YAG), erbium-doped alumina (Er:Al₂O₃), and a gas mixture dominated by carbon dioxide (CO₂). (5 points)

• Start by making a table of the most common pumping wavelengths (if the gain medium is optically pumped), lasing wavelengths (list peak gain wavelength, as well as the gain range), absorption/emission cross sections, and the pumping mechanisms of these gain materials.

• Calculate the quantum defects (q values) of these laser gain media for their main pumping wavelengths. Which gain material and pumping scheme generates least amount of heat?

• Study next how these gain materials heat up during pumping, using

T(r)=T₀+Pₕeat4 π κ L ( 1-(r²)/(R²) ) , Δ T ≈ P_( heat)4 π κ L , σ ≈ E α Δ T ,

assuming cracking at σ_fracture = 100 MPa and L=2 mm. Calculate at which pump power levels the solid-state gain materials start thermally cracking. Which gain material allows the highest pump power?

• Explain in a few sentences how heating affects gas lasers, such as the CO₂ laser.

• Mention a few approaches to reduce detrimental effects of gain-material heating, used in modern high-power laser technologies.
1.2:
1.2.
Consider four different laser types: bulk solid-state lasers, gas lasers, fiber lasers, and integrated photonic lasers. (6 points)

• What kind of output power levels one can approximately achieve using these different laser types?

• Explain qualitatively how the threshold inversion Δ N_c depends on the cavity losses γ, the gain medium length L, and the emission cross section σ. List at least three different strategies to reduce the threshold of a laser system, and briefly explain the physical idea behind each.

• Explain using your own words why the inversion threshold doesn't depend on the transverse area of the pumping beam. What quantities would depend on the transverse area of the beam?

• Estimate typical values of Δ N_c for the considered laser types. Use L_fiber=10 m, L_gas=1 m, L_bulk=1 cm, Lᵢnt=1 mm; α_fiber≈α_gas=0.1 dB/m, α_bulk=1 dB/m, αᵢnt=1 dB/cm; a linear two-mirror cavity with mirror reflectivities of 99% and 95%, negligible other single-pass losses.

• Estimate which of these parameters (L, α, γ, σ) is typically easiest to engineer in these different laser types?

• Explain why fiber lasers can operate efficiently despite having much smaller emission cross sections. Why are long, low-σ systems preferred over short, high-σ systems for high-power lasers?

• Explain what challenges exist when increasing the emission cross section of gain materials.

Consider the energy level scheme where atoms are raised from level 0 to level 2 at a pump rate Rₚ. The lifetimes of levels 1 and 2 are τ₁ and τ₂, respectively. Assuming the ground state 0 is not depleted, neglecting stimulated emission, and assuming levels 1 and 2 have the same degeneracy: (5 points)

• Write the rate equations for the population densities, N₁ and N₂.

• Calculate N₁ and N₂ as a function of time.

• Plot the population densities in the two cases: I) τ₁=2 μs, τ₂=1 μs, and II) τ₁=1 μs, τ₂=2 μs. How do the two cases differ?

Let's investigate the very important properties of laser beams, namely the spatial coherence and brightness. (4 points)

• At the surface of the Earth the intensity of the sun is approximately 1 kWm⁻². Calculate the intensity at the retina resulting from directly looking at the sun via bare eyes. Assume that the pupil of a bright-adapted eye is 2 mm in diameter, the focal length of the eye is 22.5 mm and that direct sunlight has a spatial coherence radius of approximately 80λ.

HINT: Assume that the human eye is an ideal optical system and thus conserves étendue G= AΩ, where A is the cross-sectional area and Ω is the solid angle of the incident beam of light.

• Compare the intensity to the case of looking into a 1 mW He-Ne laser (λ=632.8 nm) with a 2 mm diameter.

• Explain using a few sentences what are Class 2 lasers, and how they are still considered as eye-safe light sources. Why is this classification restricted to visible light wavelength range of 400--700 nm?

Calculate the photon flux (photons m⁻² s⁻¹) for a monochromatic plane wave of intensity I= 300 W m⁻² for wavelengths of 500 nm and 100 nm. Discuss of the difference between the results.
2.2:
2.2.
Homogeneously broadened transition of a gain medium has an unsaturated gain g₀=5.0 m⁻¹ and a saturation intensity value Iₛ=10 Wm⁻². An electromagnetic field, with a frequency resonant with the gain transition and intensity I=24 Wm⁻², propagates through this gain medium. The gain medium is 4 cm long. (5 points)

• Calculate the intensity of the amplified electromagnetic field at the medium output in the presence of constant (not saturated) gain.

• Calculate the intensity of the amplified field at the medium output in the presence of saturation, allowing the gain to depend on both propagation distance z, and the intensity I (g=g(z,I)).

• Comment on the difference between the above two results.
2.3:
2.3.
Study more quantitatively the different broadening mechanisms affecting atomic transition linewidths of gain materials. For conceptual clarity, restrict to gaseous gain media and processes of collision and Doppler broadening, affecting the natural linewidths of laser transitions of e.g. CO₂ lasers. However, note that these considerations apply directly also to other gas lasers, and on a conceptual level also to other laser types, such as to solid-state lasers. (5 points)

• Start by estimating the natural linewidth of the CO₂ laser transition near 10.6 μm. The laser transitions actually consist of a family of a closely-spaced rovibrational transitions, forming a frequency-comb like spectrum. Here, we are interested in the natural linewidth of a single rovibrational transition. (HINT: The natural linewidth is inversely proportional to the Einstein coefficient A, where the dipole moment can be calculated using bond length value of a=0.1 nm. Note that natural linewidths of molecular transitions at long-wavelelength infrared region (LWIR) are quite narrow, around 1000 Hz.)

• Consider next the collision broadening in ambient conditions (T=298 K, P=1.01325 bar). Under the hard-sphere model of a gas, collisional lifetime is given by

τ_c=((2)/(3))^(1 / 2) (1)/(8 π) (m k_B T)^(1 / 2)P a² ,

where m is the atomic mass of the CO₂ molecule. Calculate the linewidth due to collisional broadening. (HINT: value is around 300 MHz.)

• Finally, calculate the Doppler linewidth broadening, that can be estimated using

Δ ν_Doppler=2 ν₀^(1 / 2) .

What are the total linewidths and lifetimes of the CO₂ molecules taking into account all these three above contributions? (HINT: The values are around 339 MHz and 47 ns.)

Calculate the ABCD matrix for a thick and bi-convex spherical lens, surrounded by air. The lens thickness is d, and radius of curvature is R₁ (R₂) for the front (back) surface. The refractive index of the lens material is n. (7 points)

• Calculate first the ABCD matrix for a ray entering the front surface. (HINT: The standard sign convention for a convex interface requires R₁>0.)

• Calculate next the effective transfer matrix of the thick lens. Show that the thin lens limit (d → 0) results in a case where the distance of the ray from the optical axis y is not modified when propagating through the lens.
(HINT: Form and multiply together the three relevant ABCD matrices, two for the spherical interfaces, and one for the propagation inside a medium of refractive index n.)

• Verify that the final result complies with the lensmaker's equation

(1)/(f)=(n-1)((1)/(R₁)-(1)/(R₂)+((n-1) d)/(n R₁ R₂)) ,

implicitly assuming that d ≪ Rᵢ.
(HINT: The focal length is given by f = -1/C.)

Consider a resonator made of two concave mirrors (R₁>0, R₂>0) spaced by distance L. Find the values of L for which the resonator is stable.

The mirrors of a Fabry--Pérot interferometer have 95 % intensity reflectivities (identical mirrors) and the nominal length of the interferometer can be chosen to be 2 cm, 5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm, and 50 cm. The position of the other mirror can be moved around the nominal length, allowing to measure the frequency spectrum of broadband light passing through the interferometer. The light source emits a spectrum with a total bandwidth of 500 MHz. (5 points)

• What should the nominal length of the interferometer be in order to measure the spectrum as accurately as possible?

• For the above case, calculate the finesse of the cavity and the spectral resolution of the interferometer.

A diode laser emits a highly elliptical beam of blue light (λ=405 nm) with beam waist values of w_(x,0)=1 mm and w_(y,0)=2 μm along the two principal axes x and y. (5 points)

• Calculate the beam widths wₓ(z) and w_(y)(z) after propagation of 2 meters.

• Calculate the divergence angles along each axis.

• Calculate the beam aspect ratios at the source plane (the aspect ratio of the beam waists), and at the plane after propagation of 2 m.

• Find the distance at which the beam becomes a circular beam.

• Comment how this kind of strongly elliptical beam could be transformed into a circular beam.

Ring-laser gyroscopes (RLGs) consists of laser cavities where two beams propagate in opposite directions around a closed path. Modern navigation-grade RLGs are commonly based on either square or triangular ring cavities. Rotation of the cavity (the Sagnac effect) causes a phase shift

Δ φ ≈ (8 π)/(λ c) ω A

in the measured interference fringes between the clockwise (CW) and counter-clockwise (CCW) beams, where A is the enclose area of the ring, and ω is the gyroscope's rotation rate. (6 points)

• Mention a few applications for RLGs and explain why it is advantageous for an RLG to operate in a single longitudinal mode.

• If a square RLG of side length ℓ=0.4 m is formed, and the laser gain bandwidth is 100 GHz, estimate how many longitudinal modes fit within the gain profile.

• An intracavity etalon can be used to achieve single-longitudinal mode operation. If the etalon is 1 mm thick (refractive index of 1.5), what is the required finesse of the etalon?

An erbium-doped fiber laser operating near 1550 nm is formed by constructing a Fabry--Pérot resonator using two fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs). The high-reflectivity grating has a reflectivity of 99 %, and the output coupling grating has a reflectivity of 20 %. Assume that the erbium-doped fiber is the only source of internal loss and has an internal loss factor of Lᵢ=0.98 per pass. The emission cross section of erbium at 1550 nm is σ=2 × 10⁻²⁵ m² (assuming pump wavelength of 980 nm). (4 points)

• Calculate the logarithmic loss per pass γ of the resonator.

• Determine the minimum gain-fiber length required to reach the critical inversion density N_c.

In a three-level laser scheme the lower laser level is the ground state and pumping occurs through a pump band which populates, by fast relaxation, the upper laser level. Assume total population Nₜ of the active species, an upper level life-time of τ, a cavity photon lifetime τ_c, a total logarithmic loss γ, a stimulated emission cross-section σₑ of laser transition, and a length ℓ of the active medium. (6 points)

• Write the space-independent rate equations for the three-level laser. (HINT: Note that the (volumetric) pumping rate Rₚ now depends on the ground-state population.)

Your essay may briefly describe how optical elements and free-space propagation are represented using matrices, and explain how the formalism is used to analyze Gaussian beam propagation and laser resonators. Include a few practical examples of applications in laser science, such as laser cavity stability analysis, resonator design, beam shaping/focusing systems.
